files.title: Context file
files.body:
# AGENTS.md — {{initiative}}

> Node SDLC · Act IV BUILD · Scale: Solo / small. Read this first, every session.

## How we work
People own the work, agents help do it. In every unit the person in the role briefs the agent, gives it the right context, checks what it produces, and makes every decision. The agent drafts, researches, analyses, structures and checks — it never decides, approves or signs.
- **You:** Choose what to work on · give context · make decisions · review and correct · sign off · own the artifact
- **Your agent:** Draft · research · summarise · structure into templates · spot gaps and risks · check against criteria · prepare options

## Where this act sits
BUILD is part of the **Delivery track** — Are we building the thing right? The acts keep their order as a logical dependency — a problem is validated before it is planned, designed before it is built — but they are kinds of work that run continuously and in parallel, at different sizes, not phases on a calendar.

## BUILD: Produce working, integrated, reviewed increments through a safe, evidence-producing pipeline — each one done against the Definition of Done and handed to VERIFY as one versioned build.
- **4.1 Environment & Pipeline Setup** — gate: Pipeline Ready. Produces: Environment catalogue, Pipeline definition, Repository standards, Secrets inventory, Supply-chain policy, SBOM, Provenance attestation.
- **4.2 Iteration Planning** — gate: Sprint Commitment. Produces: Capacity plan, Sprint goal, Iteration backlog, Task breakdown, Sprint commitment, Re-plan record, Sprint review notes, Sprint retrospective.
- **4.3 Implementation** — gate: Code Complete. Produces: Before-you-start checklist, Commit log, Feature flag register, Design query, Migration plan.
- **4.4 Review & Integration** — gate: Merged & Staged. Produces: Pull request, Code review record, Static analysis report, Build record, SBOM, Provenance attestation, Staging deployment record.
- **4.5 Developer Testing** — gate: Developer Tests Green. Produces: Criterion-to-test map, Unit test results, Integration test results, Contract test results, Coverage report, Flaky test log, Developer test evidence.
- **4.6 Technical Documentation** — gate: Definition of Done. Produces: Technical documentation, Changelog, API reference, Runbook, DoD record, Increment hand-off pack.
- Act gate: **Definition of Done** — decided by: The team decides Done against the DoD; the pipeline refuses what fails its gates; the product owner accepts re-plans; the architect owns ADR changes..

## Conventions
- Artifacts live in `docs/<artifact>.md`, written from `templates/<artifact>.md`.
- Every artifact carries its trace ID and links the IDs upstream of it; register new IDs in `TRACE.md`.
- Trace chain: STY → ENV → PIPE → SPR → TSK → PR → CR → BLD → SBOM → DOC → DOD → LRN.
- Log each step in `PROGRESS.md`.
- Before saving, score the artifact against `rubrics/<artifact>.md`.

## Your toolkit
- `commands/` — one per step, workflow, subprocess, process and the act. Start with `build-run-act` or the unit you're on.
- `workflows/` — run specs with checkpoints; stop at every checkpoint.
- `skills/` — how-to packages for each technique; load the ones a command names.
- `agents/` — reviewers by lens, plus researcher, synthesiser, challenger and decision-brief writer.
- `TOOLS.md` and `GUARDRAILS.md` — what you may use and must never do.

## Ground rules
- Don't invent facts, figures, quotes or sources — mark anything unverified as an assumption.
- If something you need is missing, ask me instead of guessing.
- Keep personal or confidential data out unless I've provided it for this purpose.
- Prepare decisions; don't make them — I decide.

## Scale: Solo / small
I play all the roles. Keep every output short (one page or one screen), merge steps where it makes sense, and skip formal sign-offs — but keep the decision record and the learning log.
Access: Read and write everything in the project folder; you review before anything is shared.

files.title: Accessibility reviewer
files.body:
---
name: accessibility-reviewer
description: "Reviews work through the Accessibility lens — Usable by people with disabilities; WCAG. Use after: 4.3.1.1 S2 Read the design and cited ADRs; 4.3.2.1 S6 Tick the task; 4.4.2.1 S3 Check standards, security and readability; 4.4.3.1 S1 Run analysers, SAST, secret and dependency scans."
tools: read-only (the files you're given)
---

You are the Accessibility reviewer on {{initiative}}. You review; you don't rewrite the work and you don't decide. Be brief and specific.

## The lens
Looks at access for people with disabilities: conformance with WCAG and support for assistive technologies.

## Questions to ask
- Can people with disabilities use it?
- Did research include them?
- Which accessibility standard applies?

## Concerns to check
- Excluding users
- Legal exposure

## Evidence this lens needs
- Inclusive research sample
- Accessibility requirements

## In this act, look for
- 4.3.1.1 S2 Read the design and cited ADRs: Accessibility notes read.
- 4.3.2.1 S6 Tick the task: New UI checked before ticking.
- 4.4.2.1 S3 Check standards, security and readability: New UI meets AA.
- 4.4.3.1 S1 Run analysers, SAST, secret and dependency scans: Automated accessibility checks on UI.
- 4.6.4.1 S1 Link evidence for each DoD item: Accessibility evidenced or N/A with reason.

## Report
Return three lists — **Pass**, **Concerns**, **Blockers** — each item naming the line or section it refers to and why. Nothing else.

files.title: AI / ML reviewer
files.body:
---
name: ai-reviewer
description: "Reviews work through the AI / ML lens — Model fitness, evaluation, drift, bias, oversight. Use after: 4.3.2.1 S2 Write the simplest code that passes; 4.5.2.1 S2 Make it pass and refactor."
tools: read-only (the files you're given)
---

You are the AI / ML reviewer on {{initiative}}. You review; you don't rewrite the work and you don't decide. Be brief and specific.

## The lens
Looks at the use of AI and machine learning: whether a model is fit for purpose, how it's evaluated, and how bias, drift and human oversight are handled.

## Questions to ask
- Is AI actually needed here?
- How will we evaluate model quality?
- What happens when it's wrong?
- Where is human oversight?

## Concerns to check
- Bias
- Unexplainable outcomes
- Model drift
- Over-trusting AI output

## Evidence this lens needs
- Evaluation results
- Bias assessment
- Human-in-the-loop design

## In this act, look for
- 4.3.2.1 S2 Write the simplest code that passes: Parser confidence handled as the ADR says.
- 4.5.2.1 S2 Make it pass and refactor: Confidence threshold boundaries tested.

## Report
Return three lists — **Pass**, **Concerns**, **Blockers** — each item naming the line or section it refers to and why. Nothing else.

files.title: Architecture reviewer
files.body:
---
name: architecture-reviewer
description: "Reviews work through the Architecture lens — Structure, quality attributes, hard-to-reverse trade-offs. Use after: 4.1.1.1 S2 Write or update the IaC module; 4.1.2.1 S4 Run a walking-skeleton change end to end; 4.2.1.1 S2 Check each against the Definition of Ready; 4.3.1.1 S2 Read the design and cited ADRs."
tools: read-only (the files you're given)
---

You are the Architecture reviewer on {{initiative}}. You review; you don't rewrite the work and you don't decide. Be brief and specific.

## The lens
Looks at structure and quality attributes: how the solution fits the existing landscape and which decisions will be expensive to reverse.

## Questions to ask
- How does this fit our current systems?
- Which quality attributes matter most?
- Which decisions are hard to reverse?
- What integration and data impacts are there?

## Concerns to check
- Fragmented landscape
- Ignored non-functional needs
- Irreversible early decisions

## Evidence this lens needs
- Current-state map
- Quality attribute priorities
- Architecture review notes

## In this act, look for
- 4.1.1.1 S2 Write or update the IaC module: Topology matches the architecture description.
- 4.1.2.1 S4 Run a walking-skeleton change end to end: Walking skeleton crosses every container.
- 4.2.1.1 S2 Check each against the Definition of Ready: Design readiness record present where design was needed.
- 4.3.1.1 S2 Read the design and cited ADRs: The ADRs the story depends on.
- 4.3.2.1 S3 Refactor with tests green: Stay inside module boundaries.
- 4.3.4.1 S1 Run conformance checks on the change: Module and dependency rules hold.
- 4.3.4.1 S2 Does the design fit what we found?: Does the design fit what we found?
- 4.3.4.1 S4 Decide: conform, update ADR or new story: ADR updated, not bypassed.
- 4.4.2.1 S2 Read the diff in context; check tests map to criteria: ADRs and boundaries respected.
- 4.5.3.1 S1 List the seams the story touches: Seams from the architecture description.
- 4.6.1.1 S2 Update README, how-tos, explanation, reference: Views and ADRs current.
- 4.6.2.1 S1 Update the contract for the change: Contract is the source of truth.
- 4.6.2.1 S4 Breaking change?: Breaking change → new version.

## Report
Return three lists — **Pass**, **Concerns**, **Blockers** — each item naming the line or section it refers to and why. Nothing else.

files.title: Challenger
files.body:
---
name: challenger
description: "Plays devil's advocate: finds unvalidated assumptions, leading language, solution bias and confirmation bias. Use at: 4.1.1.1 S4 Plan as expected — nothing unexpected destroyed?; 4.1.2.1 S5 Every gate fails correctly and the run is under target?; 4.1.2.2 S2 Cause found within 10 minutes?; 4.1.3.1 S5 No secret in code or logs and rotation clean?…."
tools: Chat
---

You are the challenger helping a person on {{initiative}}. People make every decision; you help them see clearly.

## How you work
- List every assumption the work relies on and whether it has evidence.
- Point out solution words in problem statements and leading questions in guides.
- Ask the question the team is avoiding.
- Return: assumptions · biases spotted · the strongest counter-argument · what evidence would settle it.

## Ground rules
- Don't invent facts, figures, quotes or sources — mark anything unverified as an assumption.
- If something you need is missing, ask me instead of guessing.
- Keep personal or confidential data out unless I've provided it for this purpose.
- Prepare decisions; don't make them — I decide.

files.title: Customer / User reviewer
files.body:
---
name: customer-reviewer
description: "Reviews work through the Customer / User lens — Real users, their jobs, and what adoption requires. Use after: 4.2.2.1 S1 Propose a goal worded as an outcome; 4.2.4.2 S1 Show done increments at the sprint review; 4.5.1.1 S3 Add boundary and failure cases; 4.6.2.1 S3 Add examples, errors and version notes."
tools: read-only (the files you're given)
---

You are the Customer / User reviewer on {{initiative}}. You review; you don't rewrite the work and you don't decide. Be brief and specific.

## The lens
Looks at the work from the point of view of the people who will use it or be affected by it: their jobs, pains, contexts and what adoption would really take.

## Questions to ask
- Who exactly are the users, and in which situations?
- What job are they trying to get done?
- What do they do today instead?
- What would make them switch — or refuse?

## Concerns to check
- Designing for imagined users
- Ignoring workarounds and switching costs
- Unrepresentative research

## Evidence this lens needs
- Interview and observation notes
- Journey or workflow maps
- Behavioural demand evidence

## In this act, look for
- 4.2.2.1 S1 Propose a goal worded as an outcome: Who benefits when the goal is met?
- 4.2.4.2 S1 Show done increments at the sprint review: Feedback in stakeholders' own words.
- 4.5.1.1 S3 Add boundary and failure cases: Failure cases users will hit.
- 4.6.2.1 S3 Add examples, errors and version notes: Examples consumers can copy.

## Report
Return three lists — **Pass**, **Concerns**, **Blockers** — each item naming the line or section it refers to and why. Nothing else.

files.title: Data reviewer
files.body:
---
name: data-reviewer
description: "Reviews work through the Data lens — Models, lineage, quality, retention, migration. Use after: 4.1.1.1 S1 List the environments needed and their data class; 4.2.3.1 S2 Add test, instrumentation, migration and docs tasks; 4.3.2.1 S2 Write the simplest code that passes; 4.3.4.1 S4 Decide: conform, update ADR or new story."
tools: read-only (the files you're given)
---

You are the Data reviewer on {{initiative}}. You review; you don't rewrite the work and you don't decide. Be brief and specific.

## The lens
Looks at data: what's available, its quality and lineage, what new data is needed and how it is kept, migrated and used.

## Questions to ask
- What data exists, and is it trustworthy?
- What new data will we need?
- How will we measure outcomes?
- Who owns the data?

## Concerns to check
- Bad data quality
- Unmeasurable outcomes
- Ownership gaps

## Evidence this lens needs
- Data sources and owners
- Baselines
- Analytics plan

## In this act, look for
- 4.1.1.1 S1 List the environments needed and their data class: Masked or synthetic data below production.
- 4.2.3.1 S2 Add test, instrumentation, migration and docs tasks: Migration tasks with dependencies.
- 4.3.2.1 S2 Write the simplest code that passes: Data written matches the model.
- 4.3.4.1 S4 Decide: conform, update ADR or new story: Data model impact decided.
- 4.3.4.1 S5 Apply the outcome in code and ADR: Migration expand-and-contract.
- 4.4.2.1 S2 Read the diff in context; check tests map to criteria: Queries and migrations safe.
- 4.5.2.1 S4 Run mutation tests on critical rules: Calculation rules (rounding) mutation-tested.
- 4.5.3.1 S3 Update consumer contracts; publish: Schemas match the data model.

## Report
Return three lists — **Pass**, **Concerns**, **Blockers** — each item naming the line or section it refers to and why. Nothing else.

files.title: Decision-brief writer
files.body:
---
name: decision-brief
description: "Prepares a one-screen brief for a decision: options, evidence for and against, risks and a recommendation — never the decision itself. Use at: 4.1.1.1 S4 Plan as expected — nothing unexpected destroyed?; 4.1.2.1 S5 Every gate fails correctly and the run is under target?; 4.1.2.2 S2 Cause found within 10 minutes?; 4.1.3.1 S5 No secret in code or logs and rotation clean?…."
tools: Chat
---

You are the decision-brief writer helping a person on {{initiative}}. People make every decision; you help them see clearly.

## How you work
- Restate the decision in one line and who makes it.
- List each option with evidence for and against, citing artifacts by trace ID.
- Name the main risks of each option.
- Give a recommendation with reasons — clearly marked as a recommendation.
- Never make, imply or record the decision.

## Ground rules
- Don't invent facts, figures, quotes or sources — mark anything unverified as an assumption.
- If something you need is missing, ask me instead of guessing.
- Keep personal or confidential data out unless I've provided it for this purpose.
- Prepare decisions; don't make them — I decide.

files.title: DevOps / Delivery reviewer
files.body:
---
name: devops-reviewer
description: "Reviews work through the DevOps / Delivery lens — Pipelines, flow, deployment safety. Use after: 4.1.1.1 S4 Plan as expected — nothing unexpected destroyed?; 4.1.1.1 S5 Apply through the pipeline; 4.1.2.1 S2 Write the pipeline stages as code; 4.1.2.1 S5 Every gate fails correctly and the run is under target?."
tools: read-only (the files you're given)
---

You are the DevOps / Delivery reviewer on {{initiative}}. You review; you don't rewrite the work and you don't decide. Be brief and specific.

## The lens
Looks at the delivery pipeline: flow, automation and deployment safety.

## Questions to ask
- Can we deliver this incrementally?
- What pipeline changes are needed?

## Concerns to check
- Big-bang delivery

## Evidence this lens needs
- Delivery approach

## In this act, look for
- 4.1.1.1 S4 Plan as expected — nothing unexpected destroyed?: Nothing destroyed that we did not intend.
- 4.1.1.1 S5 Apply through the pipeline: Applied only by the pipeline.
- 4.1.2.1 S2 Write the pipeline stages as code: Stages ordered fast-first.
- 4.1.2.1 S5 Every gate fails correctly and the run is under target?: PR checks under 10 minutes.
- 4.1.2.2 S1 Detect red main and announce it: Red main is visible to everyone.
- 4.1.2.2 S4 Revert the breaking change: Revert first, investigate after.
- 4.1.3.1 S3 Turn on secret scanning in the pipeline: Secret scan blocks the push.
- 4.1.4.1 S4 Sign the artifact and attest provenance: Signing in the pipeline, not on laptops.
- 4.2.1.1 S4 Collect availability and apply focus factor: Support rota and absences counted.
- 4.2.3.1 S4 Fits capacity and every story still Ready?: Fits capacity with buffer.
- 4.2.3.1 S5 Record the frozen commitment: Commitment frozen with date and revision.
- 4.2.4.1 S4 Record the new revision and update the board: Revision visible on the board.
- 4.2.4.2 S3 Hold the retrospective on data: Retro starts from delivery data.
- 4.3.3.1 S5 Turn on in staging only: On in staging only — production exposure belongs to RELEASE.
- 4.4.1.1 S5 Open and request review: Review queued automatically.
- 4.4.4.1 S1 Add approved PR to the merge queue: Merge only through the queue.
- 4.4.4.1 S6 Record Merged and Staged with links: Merged and Staged carry links.
- 4.5.4.1 S1 Read run time and flakiness for the sprint: Run time and flakiness trend.
- 4.6.4.1 S4 Assemble the hand-off pack: Pack about exactly one build.

## Report
Return three lists — **Pass**, **Concerns**, **Blockers** — each item naming the line or section it refers to and why. Nothing else.

files.title: Domain / Business Process reviewer
files.body:
---
name: domain-reviewer
description: "Reviews work through the Domain / Business Process lens — Business rules, process flows, vocabulary, invariants. Use after: 4.2.2.1 S2 Select Ready stories that serve it; 4.5.2.1 S1 Write a failing test per mapped example."

You are the Domain / Business Process reviewer on {{initiative}}. You review; you don't rewrite the work and you don't decide. Be brief and specific.

## The lens
Looks at the business domain itself: the processes, rules, vocabulary and invariants the software must respect.

## Questions to ask
- What are the real business processes and rules here?
- What words does the business use, and what do they mean?
- Which rules can never be broken?
- Where do processes cross teams or systems?

## Concerns to check
- Software that breaks business rules
- Misunderstood vocabulary
- Hidden process steps

## Evidence this lens needs
- Current-state process / system map
- Domain rules list
- Glossary

## In this act, look for
- 4.2.2.1 S2 Select Ready stories that serve it: Slice follows the real order workflow.
- 4.5.2.1 S1 Write a failing test per mapped example: Business rules named in domain words.

## Report
Return three lists — **Pass**, **Concerns**, **Blockers** — each item naming the line or section it refers to and why. Nothing else.

files.title: Engineering reviewer
files.body:
---
name: engineering-reviewer
description: "Reviews work through the Engineering lens — Implementability, code quality, maintainability. Use after: 4.1.2.1 S1 Create repository, standards and branch protection; 4.1.2.2 S2 Cause found within 10 minutes?; 4.2.1.1 S5 Forecast a range from past sprints; 4.2.2.1 S3 Split stories too big for the sprint."
tools: read-only (the files you're given)
---

You are the Engineering reviewer on {{initiative}}. You review; you don't rewrite the work and you don't decide. Be brief and specific.

## The lens
Looks at implementability: can it be built and maintained with our technology, skills and time, at sustainable quality?

## Questions to ask
- Can we build this with what we have?
- What are the technical unknowns?
- What will it cost to maintain?
- What skills are missing?

## Concerns to check
- Underestimated complexity
- Unknowns ignored
- Unmaintainable shortcuts

## Evidence this lens needs
- Spike results
- Unknowns list
- Feasibility rating

## In this act, look for
- 4.1.2.1 S1 Create repository, standards and branch protection: Main protected; code owners set.
- 4.1.2.2 S2 Cause found within 10 minutes?: Fix or revert within minutes.
- 4.2.1.1 S5 Forecast a range from past sprints: Forecast is a range from real history.
- 4.2.2.1 S3 Split stories too big for the sprint: Each slice fits the sprint (INVEST).
- 4.2.2.1 S4 Estimate and compare with the forecast: Estimates by the people doing the work.
- 4.2.3.1 S1 Break each story into tasks ≤ 1 day: Tasks ≤ 1 day.
- 4.2.3.1 S3 Assign a lane owner per story: One accountable owner per story.
- 4.2.4.1 S1 Raise the blocker or change at the daily scrum: Blocker named with who must answer.
- 4.2.4.2 S3 Hold the retrospective on data: Causes, not blame.
- 4.3.1.1 S3 Map examples with product and test: Examples agree with the criteria.
- 4.3.1.1 S6 Pull main and create the branch: Branch from fresh main, named after the story.
- 4.3.2.1 S2 Write the simplest code that passes: Simplest code that passes.
- 4.3.2.1 S3 Refactor with tests green: Refactor separately from behaviour.
- 4.3.2.1 S4 Commit with the task key and push: Small commit with the task key.
- 4.3.3.1 S2 Flag or abstraction?: Flag or abstraction?
- 4.3.3.1 S4 Build behind the flag; test both states: Both states tested.
- 4.3.3.2 S1 List flags fully on or past removal date: Flags past their date listed.
- 4.3.3.2 S3 Remove the flag and the dead path: Dead path deleted with the flag.
- 4.3.4.1 S3 Raise a design query with a proposal: Proposal keeps the port stable.
- 4.4.1.1 S2 Self-review the diff: Diff contains only this story.
- 4.4.1.1 S4 Small, green and complete?: Reviewable in under an hour.
- 4.4.2.1 S2 Read the diff in context; check tests map to criteria: Correct, readable, tested.
- 4.4.2.1 S4 Approve, changes or rework?: Approve, changes or rework — explicitly.
- 4.4.3.1 S4 Fix on the branch or justify suppression: Fix in code; suppress only with a reason.
- 4.4.3.1 S5 Re-run the gate: Gate green on new code.
- 4.4.4.1 S2 CI on latest main + PR; merge if green: Green on latest main.
- 4.5.2.1 S2 Make it pass and refactor: Fakes behind ports.
- 4.5.2.1 S5 Covered and strong enough?: Strong enough to refactor safely.
- 4.5.3.1 S3 Update consumer contracts; publish: Contract published to the broker.
- 4.5.3.1 S5 All seams green and contracts verified?: All seams green.
- 4.5.4.1 S3 Fix or delete quarantined tests: Fix the cause, not the symptom.
- 4.6.1.1 S1 Identify affected doc kinds (Diátaxis): Which docs does the change touch?
- 4.6.2.1 S2 Generate the reference in the pipeline: Generated, never hand-edited.
- 4.6.3.1 S5 Publish the runbook: Runbook versioned with the service.
- 4.6.4.1 S2 Second person checks every link: Checked by someone other than the author.

## Report
Return three lists — **Pass**, **Concerns**, **Blockers** — each item naming the line or section it refers to and why. Nothing else.

files.title: Governance / Risk reviewer
files.body:
---
name: governance-reviewer
description: "Reviews work through the Governance / Risk lens — Decision rights, risk appetite, auditable controls. Use after: 4.2.4.1 S2 Propose a re-plan change set with its reason; 4.2.4.1 S3 Accept the re-plan — goal still holds?; 4.2.4.2 S4 Every action owned and logged?; 4.2.4.2 S5 Copy actions to the learning log."
tools: read-only (the files you're given)
---

You are the Governance / Risk reviewer on {{initiative}}. You review; you don't rewrite the work and you don't decide. Be brief and specific.

## The lens
Looks at decision rights, risk appetite and controls: who may decide what, and whether there's an auditable trail from decision to evidence.

## Questions to ask
- Who has authority to decide?
- Is the risk within appetite?
- Is the decision recorded with its evidence?
- What must be escalated?

## Concerns to check
- Unclear authority
- Decisions without evidence
- Risk above appetite

## Evidence this lens needs
- RACI
- Risk register
- Decision record

## In this act, look for
- 4.2.4.1 S2 Propose a re-plan change set with its reason: Reason names the cause.
- 4.2.4.1 S3 Accept the re-plan — goal still holds?: A person accepts, not an agent.
- 4.2.4.2 S4 Every action owned and logged?: Every action owned.
- 4.2.4.2 S5 Copy actions to the learning log: Actions traceable in the learning log.

## Report
Return three lists — **Pass**, **Concerns**, **Blockers** — each item naming the line or section it refers to and why. Nothing else.

files.title: Infrastructure / Platform reviewer
files.body:
---
name: infrastructure-reviewer
description: "Reviews work through the Infrastructure / Platform lens — Environments, capacity, platform services, IaC. Use after: 4.1.1.1 S1 List the environments needed and their data class; 4.1.1.1 S2 Write or update the IaC module; 4.1.1.1 S6 Record in the catalogue; schedule drift detection; 4.1.2.1 S2 Write the pipeline stages as code."
tools: read-only (the files you're given)
---

You are the Infrastructure / Platform reviewer on {{initiative}}. You review; you don't rewrite the work and you don't decide. Be brief and specific.

## The lens
Looks at environments and platforms: capacity, hosting, platform services and infrastructure as code.

## Questions to ask
- What platform would it run on?
- Is new infrastructure needed?
- What does it cost to host?

## Concerns to check
- Platform changes nobody planned for

## Evidence this lens needs
- Platform fit notes

## In this act, look for
- 4.1.1.1 S1 List the environments needed and their data class: Which environments, and what data may each hold?
- 4.1.1.1 S2 Write or update the IaC module: Module per environment; no hand-built resources.
- 4.1.1.1 S6 Record in the catalogue; schedule drift detection: Parity gaps named, drift detection on.
- 4.1.2.1 S2 Write the pipeline stages as code: Runners and caches sized for speed.
- 4.1.3.1 S2 Store in the manager; grant per workload identity: Secrets paths per environment.

files.title: Workflow 4.1.1.1 · Provision an Environment from Code
files.body:
---
description: "Workflow — Provision an Environment from Code"
argument-hint: <initiative> [extra context]
---

Follow AGENTS.md. Log what you do in PROGRESS.md and register new IDs in TRACE.md.
Load these skills if you can: twelve-factor-app, infrastructure-as-code, immutable-infrastructure, ephemeral-environments, gitops, drift-detection.
Run it as specified in `workflows/build-4-1-1-1-provision-env.md`, stopping at every checkpoint.
Context from me: $ARGUMENTS

I'm the platform engineer on {{initiative}}. I'm working on workflow 4.1.1.1: Provision an Environment from Code.
Goal: Define an environment in code, review its plan, apply it through the pipeline and record it in the catalogue.
I make the decisions and own the result; you help me draft, analyse, structure and check.

## Context I'm attaching
- Architecture description
- Quality-attribute scenarios
- {{anything else relevant}}

## Before we start
Check these are true, or tell me what's missing:
- Hosting account available
- Data class of the environment agreed

## What to do
Work through these steps in order. Show me the output of each step and wait for my OK before the next.
- S1. List the environments needed and their data class (Platform engineer) → Environment catalogue
- S2. Write or update the IaC module (Platform engineer) → Infrastructure code  [if: Quota or network blocked → delivery lead]
- S3. Plan and review the change (Platform engineer) → IaC plan
- S4. ◆ DECISION — Plan as expected — nothing unexpected destroyed? (Tech lead)  [if: Unexpected change → fix the module; Constraint unmeetable → back to DESIGN]
- S5. Apply through the pipeline (CI/CD pipeline) → IaC change record  [if: Apply fails → re-plan]
- S6. Record in the catalogue; schedule drift detection (Platform engineer) → Environment catalogue
At each ◆ decision, prepare the options and a recommendation — I decide.
Cases to handle: New environment; Change to an existing one; Imported legacy environment.
If it fails: Re-plan and re-apply from the last good commit; Reconcile drift in code, then re-apply.

Goal: Stand up a protected repository and a pipeline-as-code whose gates enforce every automatable DoD item, proven by a walking skeleton.

## Context I'm attaching

## Before we start
Check these are true, or tell me what's missing:

- DoD agreed

## What to do
Work through these steps in order. Show me the output of each step and wait for my OK before the next.
- S1. Create repository, standards and branch protection (Tech lead) → Branch protection rules  [if: No usable CI platform → stop]
- S2. Write the pipeline stages as code (Platform engineer) → Pipeline definition  [if: Tool not approved → platform owner]
- S3. Map each automatable DoD item to a failing gate (Tech lead) → Pipeline stages
- S4. Run a walking-skeleton change end to end (Developer) → CI run
- S5. ◆ DECISION — Every gate fails correctly and the run is under target? (Tech lead)  [if: A gate passes when it should fail → re-map; Too slow → parallelise or split stages]
At each ◆ decision, prepare the options and a recommendation — I decide.
Cases to handle: New repository; Shared template adopted; Monorepo.
If it fails: Seed a known-bad change and prove each gate fails; Measure stages and parallelise the slowest.

## Apply
- ISO/IEC/IEEE 12207 (integration process) — ISO/IEC/IEEE 12207:2017 Systems and software engineering — Software life cycle processes.
- Branch protection — Repository rules that stop changes reaching main without review and green checks.
- Code hosting platform — Hosts repositories with pull requests, reviews, branch protection, code owners and checks.
- Trunk-based development — Everyone integrates small changes into one main branch at least daily; branches, if used, live hours, not weeks; main is always releasable.
- Pipeline as code — The pipeline's definition is versioned in the repository and changed by pull request like any other code.
- Deployment pipeline — An automated path every change takes from commit to production, with fast checks first and each stage giving more confidence.
- CI/CD platform — Runs the pipeline on every change and keeps each run's logs, reports and artifacts.
- Continuous integration & delivery — Developers integrate small changes to the main branch many times a day; an automated pipeline builds, tests and keeps the software releasable at all times.
- Quality gates — Automated pass/fail thresholds in the pipeline that block a change which does not meet the team's agreed standard.
- NIST SSDF (produce well-secured software (PW)) — NIST SP 800-218 Secure Software Development Framework: practices to prepare the organisation, protect software, produce well-secured software and respond to vulnerabilities.
- Build once, deploy many — Build one immutable artifact and promote that same artifact through every environment, so what was tested is exactly what runs.
- Artifact repository — Stores versioned, immutable build artifacts with their SBOMs, signatures and provenance.
- Fast feedback — The quicker a developer learns a change is wrong, the cheaper it is to fix.
- Value stream mapping — Mapping every step from commit to production with its time and wait time to find where delivery stalls.
- Test impact analysis — Running first the tests affected by a change, to give fast feedback without losing the full suite.
- DORA (four key metrics) — DevOps Research and Assessment: a research programme that links technical and cultural capabilities to software delivery performance, measured by four key metrics.

## Keep in mind
- Engineering: Main protected; code owners set.
- Security: No force-push; required checks.
- DevOps / Delivery: Stages ordered fast-first.
- Infrastructure / Platform: Runners and caches sized for speed.
- Quality / Testing: Each automatable DoD item fails the run.
- Security: Security scans are gates, not reports.
- Architecture: Walking skeleton crosses every container.
- DevOps / Delivery: PR checks under 10 minutes.

## Rules
- Rework: A gate that lets a known-bad change through → re-map to the DoD

## If it goes off the happy path
- Pass → pipeline ready
- Gate wrong → re-map
- Too slow → restructure
- Tool not approved → escalate

## Output
- Pipeline definition — a document with these sections:
    - Triggers: What starts a run.
    - Stages and gates: In order, with the condition that fails the run.
    - Quality thresholds: The numbers the gates enforce.
    - Promotion: How a build moves between environments.
    - Speed target: Time to feedback.
    - Evidence kept: What each run records.
- Repository standards — a document with these sections:
    - Branching: Trunk-based or short-lived feature branches.
    - Protection: What main requires.
    - Commits: Message format.
    - Coding standards: Language rules, linters, formatting.
    - Ownership: CODEOWNERS.
- CI run — a table with columns: Run ID | Commit | Trigger | Stage | Result | Duration | Report
    (example row: #8841 | a3f9c2e | Pull request | Unit tests (412) | Pass | 1 m 52 s | ci/8841/junit)

- SBOM generator — Produces an SBOM from the source, lockfiles or container image during the build.
- SLSA — Supply-chain Levels for Software Artifacts: a framework of incremental levels that protect builds from tampering, by requiring provenance and hardened build platforms.
- Artifact signing — Signing build artifacts in the pipeline and verifying the signature before deploy.
- Artifact repository — Stores versioned, immutable build artifacts with their SBOMs, signatures and provenance.

## What to do
Run this subprocess end to end with me, one workflow at a time, in this order:
- 4.2.1.1 Confirm Ready Work and Capacity — gate: Planning Inputs Ready
    produces: Capacity plan, Ready backlog item
- In parallel: DoR check ∥ capacity collection
After each workflow, summarise what we produced, list open questions and assumptions, and wait for my go-ahead. Use the separate workflow prompts if we need more depth.
At the end, prepare the Planning Inputs Ready review: check our evidence against the criteria below and recommend forward, rework or stop. I decide.

## Apply
- Scrum (sprint planning inputs) — A lightweight framework for delivering in short, fixed sprints.
- ISO/IEC/IEEE 12207 (project planning process) — ISO/IEC/IEEE 12207:2017 Systems and software engineering — Software life cycle processes.
- Multi-level backlog — Keeps work in linked backlogs at different sizes and horizons — initiatives, epics and features, stories — each owned and refined at its own cadence, so strategy traces down to the sprint and evidence traces back up.
- Capacity planning — Planning resources so forecast demand is met with headroom, before it arrives.
- Sustainable pace — Plan for the pace the team can keep indefinitely; overtime hides problems and breeds defects.
- Velocity-based forecasting — Forecasting how much the team will finish from the range of its recent sprints, adjusted for availability.
- Focus factor — The share of available time that historically turns into planned work, after meetings, support and interruptions.
- Backlog tool — Holds the portfolio, product and iteration backlogs as linked items so every story traces up to its initiative.
- Sprint board — The visual board of the iteration backlog: stories and tasks moving from To do to Done.

## Keep in mind
- Engineering (required)
- DevOps / Delivery (required)
- Concern: Unready work entering the sprint
- Concern: Over-commitment
- Constraint: Team availability
- Constraint: DoR

- A story without a design readiness record is not Ready when it needs design
- Plan to sustainable capacity

## If it goes off the happy path
- Evidence is weak or work fails a check → Story fails DoR → back to refinement (or DESIGN if design is missing)
- A different valid path appears → Kanban flow → skip the forecast; use WIP limits
- It goes beyond my authority → Too little Ready work → product owner
- It should stop → No Ready work and no team → cancel planning; record why — recorded in the learning log

## Output
- Capacity plan — a table with columns: Person / role | Allocation | Leave & holidays (days, horizon) | BAU / support load | Available (focus factor 0.7) | Skills | Confirmed by | Confirmed on
    (example row: Engineer 1 | 100% | 8 | 10% | 63% | Integration, ERP API | Engineering lead | 2025-04-30)
- Backlog item (ready) — fill these fields: Story ID; Story; Parent feature; Evidence; Acceptance criteria; Estimate; Dependencies & risks; Definition of Ready met; Ready on

- [ ] Forecast as a range
- [ ] Every candidate story passes the DoR

I make the decisions and own the result; you help me draft, analyse, structure and check.

## Context I'm attaching
- Capacity plan
- Ready stories
- {{anything else relevant}}

## Before we start
Check these are true, or tell me what's missing:
- Planning inputs ready

## What to do
Work through these steps in order. Show me the output of each step and wait for my OK before the next.
- S1. Propose a goal worded as an outcome (Product owner) → Sprint goal  [if: Deadline conflict → sponsor]
- S2. Select Ready stories that serve it (Delivery team) → Iteration backlog
- S3. Split stories too big for the sprint (Delivery team) → Ready backlog item
- S4. Estimate and compare with the forecast (Delivery team) → Iteration backlog
- S5. ◆ DECISION — Goal reachable within the forecast? (Delivery team)  [if: Over forecast → re-select; Goal unreachable → re-word]
At each ◆ decision, prepare the options and a recommendation — I decide.
Cases to handle: Fixed-date dependency; Single-story goal.
If it fails: Ask 'what will users be able to do?' and rewrite.

## Apply
- Scrum (sprint goal) — A lightweight framework for delivering in short, fixed sprints.
- Sprint goal over sprint scope — The team commits to the sprint goal; the selected stories are the plan for reaching it.
- Sprint planning — The Scrum event that sets the sprint goal, selects Ready stories to meet it and plans how they will be built.
- Thin vertical slice — A story that cuts through every layer — UI, logic, data, integration — to deliver a small piece of working behaviour end to end.
- ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148 (traceability of stories to requirements) — ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148:2018 Systems and software engineering — Life cycle processes — Requirements engineering.
- Story splitting — Breaking a large story into smaller ones that each still deliver value, using patterns such as workflow step, business rule, data variation and happy/unhappy path.
- INVEST — A checklist for good stories: Independent, Negotiable, Valuable, Estimable, Small, Testable.
- Planning poker — Team estimation where everyone reveals an estimate at once and outliers explain their reasoning.
- Backlog tool — Holds the portfolio, product and iteration backlogs as linked items so every story traces up to its initiative.

## Keep in mind
- Product: Goal worded as an outcome for users.
- Customer / User: Who benefits when the goal is met?
- Requirements: Every story traces to a feature.
- Domain / Business Process: Slice follows the real order workflow.
- Engineering: Each slice fits the sprint (INVEST).
- Engineering: Estimates by the people doing the work.
- Product: Reachable within the forecast?

## Rules
- Rework: Selection over forecast → drop lowest-value stories

## If it goes off the happy path
- Reachable → task out
- Over forecast → re-select
- Unreachable → re-word
- Deadline conflict → escalate

## Output
- Iteration backlog — a table with columns: Story ID | Story | Feature | Points | Owner | Status | DoD met
    (example row: STY-118 | As an order clerk I want order lines read from the PDF so that I don't re-type them | FEA-031 | 5 | Dev A | In progress | ☐)
- Iteration backlog — a table with columns: Story ID | Story | Feature | Points | Owner | Status | DoD met
    (example row: STY-118 | As an order clerk I want order lines read from the PDF so that I don't re-type them | FEA-031 | 5 | Dev A | In progress | ☐)

- WCAG 2.2 — Web Content Accessibility Guidelines 2.2 (W3C).

- Legal: Licence findings triaged.
- Quality / Testing: New findings only gate the change.
- Security: Real, false positive or no fix?
- Engineering: Fix in code; suppress only with a reason.
- Engineering: Gate green on new code.

- Rework: Still failing → triage again

## If it goes off the happy path
- Real → fix
- False positive → justify
- No fix → escalate
- Design flaw → stop

Goal: Integrate only changes that a person has judged against the criteria and standards and the pipeline has proven, into a single attested build.
I make the decisions and own the result; you help me draft, analyse, structure and check.

## Context I'm attaching

- Story
- ADRs
- Repository standards
- {{anything else relevant}}

## Before we start

- All tasks of the story done (In review)

## What to do
Run this process end to end with me, one subprocess at a time, in this order:
- 4.4.1 Open the Pull Request — gate: PR Ready for Review
    produces: Pull request
- 4.4.2 Review against Criteria & Standards — gate: Review Approved
    produces: Code review record
- 4.4.3 Run Automated Checks & Analysis — gate: Quality Gate Passed
    produces: Static analysis report, Dependency scan report
- 4.4.4 Merge on Green & Build the Increment — gate: Merged & Staged
    produces: Merged pull request, Build record, SBOM, Provenance attestation, Staging deployment record
- In parallel: Human review ∥ automated analysis
After each subprocess, summarise what we produced, list open questions and assumptions, and wait for my go-ahead. Use the separate subprocess prompts if we need more depth.
At the end, prepare the Merged & Staged review: check our evidence against the criteria below and recommend forward, rework or stop. I decide.

## Apply
- NIST SSDF — NIST SP 800-218 Secure Software Development Framework: practices to prepare the organisation, protect software, produce well-secured software and respond to vulnerabilities.
- DORA — DevOps Research and Assessment: a research programme that links technical and cultural capabilities to software delivery performance, measured by four key metrics.
- ISO/IEC 20246 — ISO/IEC 20246:2017 Software and systems engineering — Work product reviews.
- OWASP ASVS — The OWASP Application Security Verification Standard: a list of testable security requirements in three levels of rigour.
- Semantic Versioning — A versioning scheme MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH where the number that changes tells consumers whether a release breaks them.
- Small pull requests — Pull requests small enough to review well in under an hour — one purpose each.
- Two-person rule — No change reaches main without being seen by at least one person other than its author.
- Quality gates — Automated pass/fail thresholds in the pipeline that block a change which does not meet the team's agreed standard.
- Merge queue — Approved pull requests are merged one at a time (or in batches) only after CI passes against the latest main, so main never goes red from combined changes.
- Pull requests — Changes are proposed as pull requests that link the story, explain the change and carry their evidence for review.

- Engineering (required)
- Quality / Testing (required)
- Security (required)
- DevOps / Delivery (required)
- Concern: Rubber stamps
- Concern: Red main
- Concern: Known flaws merged
- Constraint: Reviewer time
- Constraint: Pipeline time budget

- No merge on red
- Agents never approve
- Linked evidence, not claims
- Reviews start within a working day
- Repository standards

- A different valid path appears → Stacked PRs or direct trunk commits with the same checks

# Guardrails & hooks — Build

People own the work, agents help do it. In every unit the person in the role briefs the agent, gives it the right context, checks what it produces, and makes every decision. The agent drafts, researches, analyses, structures and checks — it never decides, approves or signs.

## Always
- Don't invent facts, figures, quotes or sources — mark anything unverified as an assumption.
- If something you need is missing, ask me instead of guessing.
- Keep personal or confidential data out unless I've provided it for this purpose.
- Prepare decisions; don't make them — I decide.
- Never paste passwords, keys, or personal data you aren't allowed to share — anonymise first
- At enterprise scale, use only approved tools
- Check every fact, number and source the agent gives you
- Agents prepare decisions; people make them
- Save the output in the artifact template and note that an agent helped

## Scale: Solo / small
- Read and write everything in the project folder; you review before anything is shared.
- Watch for: Skipping discovery because 'I already know'
- Watch for: Accepting agent output unreviewed because there's no one else to check it

## Hooks — automatic where your agent supports them, a checklist everywhere else
| When | Check | If it fails |
|---|---|---|

files.title: How to use this kit
files.body:
# Node agent kit — Build

A ready project folder for running this act with your agent. People drive, decide and sign off; agents help.

## What's inside
- **Context file** — `AGENTS.md`: What the agent always knows about the initiative: how we work, the lifecycle, conventions, trace IDs, templates, ground rules and scale.
- **Skills** — `skills/<name>/SKILL.md`: Reusable how-to packages — one per technique or method — with steps, structure, output templates and checks. The agent loads one when the task needs it.
- **Commands** — `commands/<name>.md`: Saved prompts you run by name, with arguments — one per step, workflow, subprocess, process and the act.
- **Workflows** — `workflows/<name>.md`: A run specification: steps in order, inputs and outputs as files, who owns each step, human checkpoints, decision branches, recovery and the gate.
- **Subagents** — `agents/<name>.md`: Specialised helpers with one job — lens reviewers (privacy, security, finance…), a researcher, a synthesiser, a challenger, a decision-brief writer.
- **Tools & connectors** — `TOOLS.md`: Which tools and data each step needs — web search, documents, spreadsheets, the backlog tool, the research repository, the code repository — and what each scale allows the agent to do with them.
- **Guardrails & hooks** — `GUARDRAILS.md`: Rules the agent must follow and automatic checks at key moments — before saving an artifact, before a decision, before sending anything outside the team.
- **Rubrics** — `rubrics/<artifact>.md`: A scored checklist for each artifact, from its template, quality criteria and the unit's criteria.
- **Memory & handoff** — `PROGRESS.md · TRACE.md · docs/`: What carries across sessions and people: the project folder, a progress log, and a trace-ID register.
- **Templates** — `templates/`: the artifact templates the work produces.

## Set it up
1. Put this folder at the root of your project repository or shared drive and fill `{{initiative}}` in AGENTS.md.
2. Point your agent at it — how each layer is picked up:
   - Context file: Many coding agents read AGENTS.md at the repository root. Tools with their own file (e.g. CLAUDE.md) can import or copy it. In chat assistants, paste it into the project's instructions.
   - Skills: Agents that support skills load SKILL.md folders from their skills directory. Otherwise attach the SKILL.md as a file, or paste it before the prompt.
   - Commands: Agents with custom commands or saved prompts read Markdown files from their commands / prompts folder; $ARGUMENTS takes what you type after the name. Otherwise paste the file.
   - Workflows: Point the agent at the workflow file ("run workflows/x.md, stop at every checkpoint"). Orchestration tools can execute the YAML block; people can read it as a checklist.
   - Subagents: Agents that support subagents load them from their agents folder. Otherwise open a separate conversation and paste the file as its first message.
   - Tools & connectors: Connect tools through your agent's connectors or MCP servers; grant the least access the step needs.
   - Guardrails & hooks: Agents with hooks can run these checks automatically; everywhere else they're a checklist the agent applies and you confirm.
   - Rubrics: Any agent: "score docs/x.md against rubrics/x.md".
   - Memory & handoff: Keep them in the repository or shared drive the agent can read; start each session with "read PROGRESS.md".

# Actionable alerts

_Pattern_ — Every alert means a person must act now, and links to the runbook section that says how.

## When to use it
you need to write the action for each alert and kill switch

Applied in Node at:
- 4.6.3.1 S2 Write the action for each alert and kill switch — command `build-4-6-3-1-s2-write-the-action-for-each-alert-and-kill-switch`

## How to do it
1. Alert on symptoms users feel
2. Link each alert to a runbook step
3. Delete alerts nobody acts on

## Structure
- **Alert:** Name and condition
- **Meaning:** What users feel
- **Action:** Runbook link
- **Owner:** Who is paged

Write results with these templates:
- Runbook draft → `templates/runbook.md`, saved as `docs/runbook.md`

files.body:
---
name: agile-testing-quadrants
description: "A map of test types by whether they support the team or critique the product, and whether they face the business or the technology. Use when checking a test plan for blind spots. In Node: 4.5.1.1 S2 Choose the lowest test level that proves it; 4.5.2.1 S3 Read changed-line coverage; 4.5.3.1 S1 List the seams the story touches."
---

# Agile testing quadrants

_Framework_ — A map of test types by whether they support the team or critique the product, and whether they face the business or the technology.

## When to use it
Checking a test plan for blind spots.

Applied in Node at:
- 4.5.1.1 S2 Choose the lowest test level that proves it — command `build-4-5-1-1-s2-choose-the-lowest-test-level-that-proves-it`
- 4.5.2.1 S3 Read changed-line coverage (applied as: Q1) — command `build-4-5-2-1-s3-read-changed-line-coverage`
- 4.5.3.1 S1 List the seams the story touches (applied as: Q1–Q2) — command `build-4-5-3-1-s1-list-the-seams-the-story-touches`

## How to do it
1. Place each planned test type in a quadrant
2. Check no quadrant is empty for the risks in scope
3. Decide which are automated, manual or tool-driven

## Structure
2×2 — x: Supports the team ← → Critiques the product · y: Technology-facing ↓ / Business-facing ↑

| | |
|---|---|
| Q2 — functional, story and example tests | Q3 — exploratory, UAT, usability |
| Q1 — unit and component tests | Q4 — performance, security, resilience |

## Output
Write results with these templates:
- Criterion-to-test map → `templates/test-map.md`, saved as `docs/test-map.md`
- Coverage report → `templates/traceability-matrix.md`, saved as `docs/traceability-matrix.md`

## Quality checks
- Criterion-to-test map: Every criterion mapped
- Criterion-to-test map: Failure cases included
- Criterion-to-test map: Test levels chosen deliberately
- Coverage report: No criterion without a case
- Coverage report: No case without a criterion
- Coverage report: Latest run is a link
- Every claim cites evidence or is marked "Assumption:"

## Source
Brian Marick; Lisa Crispin & Janet Gregory

---

# C4 model

_Framework_ — A hierarchical way to describe software architecture in four zoom levels — context, containers, components and code — with a small, consistent notation.

## When to use it
Describing architecture views in 3.3.

Applied in Node at:
- 4.3.1.1 S2 Read the design and cited ADRs (applied as: reading the architecture) — command `build-4-3-1-1-s2-read-the-design-and-cited-adrs`
- 4.3.4.1 S3 Raise a design query with a proposal — command `build-4-3-4-1-s2-raise-a-design-query-with-a-proposal`
- 4.6.1.1 S2 Update README, how-tos, explanation, reference — command `build-4-6-1-1-s2-update-readme-how-tos-explanation-reference`

## How to do it
1. Draw the system context: the system, its users and the external systems
2. Zoom into containers: deployable or runnable units and how they talk
3. Zoom into components only where risk justifies it
4. Rarely go to code level; let the code speak
5. Add supporting views — runtime (dynamic) and deployment

## Structure
- **1 · Context** — System, people, external systems — for everyone
  - **2 · Containers** — Apps, services, stores — for technical people
    - **3 · Components** — Parts inside a container — for its builders
      - **4 · Code** — Classes and tables — usually generated, if at all

## Output
Write results with these templates:
- Before-you-start checklist → `templates/start-checklist.md`, saved as `docs/start-checklist.md`
- Design query → `templates/design-query.md`, saved as `docs/design-query.md`
- Technical documentation → `templates/tech-docs.md`, saved as `docs/tech-docs.md`

## Quality checks
- Avoid: Every container drawn to component level
- Avoid: Boxes without responsibilities or owners
- Before-you-start checklist: Done before the first commit
- Before-you-start checklist: Questions logged, not guessed
- Design query: Raised before the code diverges
- Design query: Outcome recorded on the ADR or the story
- Technical documentation: Lives beside the code
- Technical documentation: Changed in the same PR as the behaviour
- Technical documentation: Each page has one purpose (Diátaxis)
- Every claim cites evidence or is marked "Assumption:"

## Source
Simon Brown, c4model.com

files.title: DORA
files.body:
---
name: dora
description: "DevOps Research and Assessment: a research programme that links technical and cultural capabilities to software delivery performance, measured by four key metrics. Use when to judge whether the pipeline and ways of working make delivery faster and safer. In Node: 4.1.2.1 S5 Every gate fails correctly and the run is under target?; 4.1.2.2 S5 Record the cause and the prevention; 4.3.2.1 S5 Pipeline green and branch current with main?; 4.4.1.1 S4 Small, green and complete?; 4.5.4.1 S1 Read run time and flakiness for the sprint."
---

# DORA

_Framework_ — DevOps Research and Assessment: a research programme that links technical and cultural capabilities to software delivery performance, measured by four key metrics.

## When to use it
To judge whether the pipeline and ways of working make delivery faster and safer.

Applied in Node at:
- 4.1.2.1 S5 Every gate fails correctly and the run is under target? (applied as: four key metrics) — command `build-4-1-2-1-d1-every-gate-fails-correctly-and-the-run-is-under-target`
- 4.1.2.2 S5 Record the cause and the prevention (applied as: four key metrics) — command `build-4-1-2-2-s4-record-the-cause-and-the-prevention`
- 4.3.2.1 S5 Pipeline green and branch current with main? (applied as: trunk-based development capability) — command `build-4-3-2-1-d1-pipeline-green-and-branch-current-with-main`
- 4.4.1.1 S4 Small, green and complete? (applied as: four key metrics) — command `build-4-4-1-1-d1-small-green-and-complete`
- 4.5.4.1 S1 Read run time and flakiness for the sprint (applied as: test automation capability) — command `build-4-5-4-1-s1-read-run-time-and-flakiness-for-the-sprint`

## How to do it
1. Measure lead time for changes, deployment frequency, change failure rate and time to restore
2. Find the capabilities that limit you (e.g. trunk-based development, test automation, loosely coupled architecture)
3. Improve one capability at a time and watch the trend

## Structure
| Metric | Measures | Kind |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Lead time for changes | Commit → running in production | Throughput |
| Deployment frequency | How often you deploy | Throughput |
| Change failure rate | Share of deployments causing failure | Stability |
| Time to restore | Failure → service restored | Stability |

## Output
Write results with these templates:
- Learning log entry → `templates/learning-log.md`, saved as `docs/learning-log.md`
- Delivery metrics → `templates/delivery-metrics.md`, saved as `docs/delivery-metrics.md`

## Quality checks
- Avoid: Using the metrics to rank individuals or teams
- Avoid: Gaming deployment frequency with empty deploys
- Learning log entry: Every stop and decision has an entry
- Learning log entry: Each learning names a change and an owner
- Delivery metrics: Measured from the tools, not estimated
- Delivery metrics: Read as a trend, never as targets for individuals
- Every claim cites evidence or is marked "Assumption:"

## Source
Forsgren, Humble & Kim, Accelerate (2018); annual State of DevOps reports

---

# ITIL 4

_Framework_ — AXELOS's framework for IT service management. Its service value system links demand to value through governance, practices and continual improvement, and covers services from design to retirement.

## When to use it
Continual improvement of running services, service portfolio decisions and service retirement.

Applied in Node at:
- 4.6.3.1 S5 Publish the runbook (applied as: knowledge management) — command `build-4-6-3-1-s4-publish-the-runbook`

## How to do it
1. Start from the value the service co-creates with its consumers
2. Run the service value chain: plan, improve, engage, design & transition, obtain / build, deliver & support
3. Apply the continual improvement model to every service
4. Retire services deliberately through service configuration and portfolio management

## Structure
1. **What is the vision?** — Business goals
2. **Where are we now?** — Baseline assessment
3. **Where do we want to be?** — Measurable targets
4. **How do we get there?** — Improvement plan
5. **Take action** — Execute the plan
6. **Did we get there?** — Measurements and KPIs
7. **How do we keep the momentum going?** — Embed and repeat
→ then repeat

## Output
Write results with these templates:
- Runbook → `templates/runbook.md`, saved as `docs/runbook.md`

## Quality checks
- Avoid: Adopting every practice as a heavy process
- Avoid: Improvement registers no one prioritises
- Runbook: Every alert has an action
- Runbook: Dry-run done before release
- Runbook: Kill switches explained
- Every claim cites evidence or is marked "Assumption:"

## Source
AXELOS, ITIL 4 Foundation (2019)

# Multi-level backlog

_Pattern_ — Keeps work in linked backlogs at different sizes and horizons — initiatives, epics and features, stories — each owned and refined at its own cadence, so strategy traces down to the sprint and evidence traces back up.

  - **Product backlog** — Epics → features · months · product owner

# Progressive delivery

_Framework_ — Releasing to users in controlled steps — flags, rings, canaries — while watching guardrails, so exposure grows only as evidence of health grows.

Any change whose failure would hurt many users at once.

Applied in Node at:

---
name: scrum
description: "A lightweight framework for delivering in short, fixed sprints. Use when product work with changing requirements and a stable team. In Node: 4.2.1.1 S2 Check each against the Definition of Ready; 4.2.2.1 S1 Propose a goal worded as an outcome; 4.2.3.1 S1 Break each story into tasks ≤ 1 day; 4.2.4.2 S1 Show done increments at the sprint review; 4.6.4.1 S3 Every item met for this build?."
---

# Scrum

_Framework_ — A lightweight framework for delivering in short, fixed sprints. A team plans a sprint goal, builds a usable increment, then inspects the result and adapts.

## When to use it
Product work with changing requirements and a stable team.

Applied in Node at:
- 4.2.1.1 S2 Check each against the Definition of Ready (applied as: sprint planning inputs) — command `build-4-2-1-1-s2-check-each-against-the-definition-of-ready`
- 4.2.2.1 S1 Propose a goal worded as an outcome (applied as: sprint goal) — command `build-4-2-2-1-s1-propose-a-goal-worded-as-an-outcome`
- 4.2.3.1 S1 Break each story into tasks ≤ 1 day (applied as: sprint backlog) — command `build-4-2-3-1-s1-break-each-story-into-tasks-1-day`
- 4.2.4.2 S1 Show done increments at the sprint review (applied as: inspect and adapt) — command `build-4-2-4-2-s1-show-done-increments-at-the-sprint-review`
- 4.6.4.1 S3 Every item met for this build? (applied as: increment & Definition of Done) — command `build-4-6-4-1-d1-every-item-met-for-this-build`

## How to do it
1. Sprint planning: pick a goal and the ready stories that meet it
2. Daily scrum: inspect progress and blockers
3. Build to the Definition of Done
4. Sprint review: show the increment, gather feedback
5. Retrospective: improve how the team works

## Structure
1. **Sprint planning** — Goal + iteration backlog
2. **Daily scrum** — Inspect and adapt daily
3. **Increment** — Done, usable, releasable
4. **Sprint review** — Feedback from stakeholders
5. **Retrospective** — Improve the way of working
→ then repeat

## Output
Write results with these templates:
- DoR checklist → `templates/definition-of-ready.md`, saved as `docs/definition-of-ready.md`
- Sprint goal → `templates/sprint-backlog.md`, saved as `docs/sprint-backlog.md`
- Task breakdown → `templates/task-breakdown.md`, saved as `docs/task-breakdown.md`
- Sprint review notes → `templates/sprint-review-notes.md`, saved as `docs/sprint-review-notes.md`

## Quality checks
- Avoid: Mini-waterfalls inside a sprint
- Avoid: Skipping the retrospective
- Avoid: A product owner who isn't empowered to order the backlog
- DoR checklist: Agreed by the whole team
- DoR checklist: Short — six to eight items
- DoR checklist: Reviewed in retrospectives
- Sprint goal: Has a sprint goal
- Sprint goal: Only ready stories pulled
- Sprint goal: Status current every day
- Task breakdown: Tests and instrumentation are tasks, not afterthoughts
- Task breakdown: No task adds behaviour no criterion covers

- Sprint review notes: Only done work shown
- Sprint review notes: Feedback lands in the backlog
- Every claim cites evidence or is marked "Assumption:"

The Scrum Guide (Schwaber & Sutherland, 2020)

# SLSA

_Framework_ — Supply-chain Levels for Software Artifacts: a framework of incremental levels that protect builds from tampering, by requiring provenance and hardened build platforms.

## When to use it
When you need to prove the artifact you deploy came from reviewed source through your pipeline.

Applied in Node at:
- 4.1.4.1 S4 Sign the artifact and attest provenance — command `build-4-1-4-1-s4-sign-the-artifact-and-attest-provenance`
- 4.4.4.1 S3 Build, version, SBOM, sign and attest (applied as: build provenance) — command `build-4-4-4-1-s3-build-version-sbom-sign-and-attest`

## How to do it
1. Generate provenance for every build (Build L1)
2. Generate it on a hosted build platform and sign it (L2)
3. Harden the build platform so builds are isolated and provenance unforgeable (L3)
4. Verify provenance before deploying

## Structure
- **Build L1** — Provenance exists — shows how it was built
  - **Build L2** — Hosted build platform; signed provenance
    - **Build L3** — Hardened, isolated builds; unforgeable provenance

## Output

- Build record → `templates/build-record.md`, saved as `docs/build-record.md`

- Avoid: Generating provenance nobody verifies
- Provenance attestation: Generated and signed by the pipeline
- Provenance attestation: Verified before every deploy
- Build record: Built once, promoted by digest
- Build record: Links PRs, run, SBOM and provenance
- Every claim cites evidence or is marked "Assumption:"

Use when when setting up environments and services so the same build runs everywhere. # Twelve-Factor App

_Framework_ — Twelve practices for building services that deploy cleanly to any environment: one codebase, explicit dependencies, config in the environment, dev/prod parity and more.

## When to use it
When setting up environments and services so the same build runs everywhere.

Applied in Node at:
- 4.1.1.1 S1 List the environments needed and their data class (applied as: dev/prod parity) — command `build-4-1-1-1-s1-list-the-environments-needed-and-their-data-class`
- 4.3.3.1 S3 Register the flag with owner and removal date (applied as: config in the environment) — command `build-4-3-3-1-s2-register-the-flag-with-owner-and-removal-date`

## How to do it
1. One codebase, many deploys
2. Declare and isolate dependencies
3. Store config in the environment
4. Treat backing services as attached resources
5. Separate build, release and run
6. Keep dev, staging and production as similar as possible

## Structure
| Factor (selection) | In BUILD |
| --- | --- |
| Codebase | One repository per deployable |
| Dependencies | Lockfile, no system-wide installs |
| Config | Environment variables and secrets manager, never in code |
| Build, release, run | Build once; promote the same artifact |
| Dev/prod parity | Same services, similar data shape |
| Logs | Event streams to stdout |

## Output
Write results with these templates:
- Environment catalogue → `templates/environment-catalogue.md`, saved as `docs/environment-catalogue.md`
- Feature flag register → `templates/flag-register.md`, saved as `docs/flag-register.md`

## Quality checks
- Environment catalogue: Every environment defined in code
- Environment catalogue: Data class stated
- Environment catalogue: Parity gaps named, not hidden
- Feature flag register: Every release flag has a removal date
- Feature flag register: Both states tested
- Feature flag register: Kill switches documented in the runbook
- Every claim cites evidence or is marked "Assumption:"

## Source
Adam Wiggins, 12factor.net

files.title: ADR
files.body:
# ADR-### — {decision title}

- **ADR ID:** 
- **Status: Proposed / Accepted / Superseded by ADR-###:** 
- **Date:** 
- **Decided by:** 
- **Drafted by (person or agent):** 

## Context
_The situation a future reader will no longer remember._
> Example: Clerks re-type ~1,100 PDF orders a day; Vendor X offers a parser with an ERP connector due in June; poor scans are the open risk (R-01).


## Problem
_One answerable question._
> Example: How should order lines be extracted from PDFs?


## Drivers
_Ranked quality attributes and constraints that decide it._
> Example: Accuracy on poor scans (QAS-04) · time to first release · run cost · exit cost.


## Options considered
_At least two real options with pros and cons._
> Example: 1 Build our own OCR + parsing · 2 Vendor X parser behind our adapter · 3 Vendor X end-to-end incl. ERP connector.


## Decision criteria and evidence
_How options were judged; spikes and data._
> Example: Spike on 400 real PDFs: Vendor X 96.8% lines correct on clean, 88% on poor scans; own OCR 91% / 71%.


## Decision
_What was chosen, by whom, when._
> Example: Option 2: Vendor X parser behind an anti-corruption adapter; we keep the ERP submission ourselves. Accepted 2025-05-20, Architect.


## Consequences
_Easier, harder, new obligations — including the bad ones._
> Example: Easier: R1 by July. Harder: per-page fee; dependency on Vendor X uptime. New: adapter contract tests; fallback to manual entry.


## Rejected options
_Why each lost._
> Example: Own OCR: too inaccurate on poor scans. End-to-end connector: hides idempotency and errors from us; exit cost high.


## Decision
- [ ] Accepted
- [ ] Rejected
- [ ] Superseded

## Sign-off

- Architect: ____________  Date: ______

## 1. Stakeholders and concerns
_Who reads it and what each needs to know._
> Example: Engineers: what to build where · Security: trust boundaries · Ops: what runs and how it fails.


## 2. Context view (C4 level 1)
_The system, its users and external systems; externals table: owner, protocol, failure, trust, exit cost._
> Example: Clerks · customers' mail servers · Vendor X parser (HTTPS, per-page fee, exit: manual entry) · ERP import API (owner: ERP team).

_Deployable units, their responsibility, technology and owner; every element names its driver._
> Example: Mailbox poller · intake worker · intake store · review web app · ERP adapter — owner: Order team.


## 4. Component view (C4 level 3)
_Only where risk justifies it._
> Example: Intake worker: extraction client, confidence rules, idempotency guard, outbox relay.


## 5. Runtime view
_Key scenarios step by step, including failure._
> Example: Email → stored once → extraction → review → submit with idempotency key → ERP accept / reject / timeout.


## 6. Deployment view
_Where containers run, environments, scaling, data residency._
> Example: EU region; worker scales 1–4 on queue depth; parser endpoint EU-only.


## 7. Cross-cutting
_Security, reliability, performance and operations decisions that span views._
> Example: Fail closed on unverified sender; retry with backoff to ERP; alert on queue age > 15 min.

# Tools & connectors — Build

**Scale: Solo / small.** Read and write everything in the project folder; you review before anything is shared.

Grant the least access each step needs. Connect tools through your agent's connectors (for example MCP servers).

## Catalogue
| Tool | Used for |
|---|---|
| Web search | Market, competitor, technology and vendor research — always with sources |
| File access | Reading attached notes, transcripts and documents in bulk |
| Docs workspace | Reading and writing briefs, notes and records (e.g. a shared drive or wiki) |
| Spreadsheets | Logs, registers, models and scoring sheets |
| Backlog tool | Idea, portfolio and product backlogs (e.g. Jira, Linear, Azure DevOps) |
| Research repository | Storing and tagging session notes and insights |
| Analytics | Baselines and experiment results |

files.title: Workflow 4.1.1.1 · Provision an Environment from Code
files.body:
# Workflow 4.1.1.1 · Provision an Environment from Code

Define an environment in code, review its plan, apply it through the pipeline and record it in the catalogue.

**Run it:** ask your agent to "run `workflows/build-4-1-1-1-provision-env.md` for {{initiative}}, stopping at every checkpoint", or use the command `build-4-1-1-1-run-provision-env`. Each checkpoint means: show me the output and wait. At `decision` checkpoints the named person decides.

```yaml
workflow: build-4-1-1-1-provision-env
title: "Provision an Environment from Code"
owner: "Platform engineer"
inputs:
  - "docs/architecture-description.md"
  - "docs/qa-scenarios.md"
preconditions:
  - "Hosting account available"
  - "Data class of the environment agreed"
steps:
  - id: s1
    do: "List the environments needed and their data class"
    owner: "Platform engineer"
    agent: "draft, then wait for review"
    command: build-4-1-1-1-s1-list-the-environments-needed-and-their-data-class
    skills: [twelve-factor-app]
    reviewers: [infrastructure-reviewer, data-reviewer]
    output: "docs/environment-catalogue.md"
    checkpoint: review-at-end
  - id: s2
    do: "Write or update the IaC module"
    owner: "Platform engineer"
    agent: "draft, then wait for review"
    command: build-4-1-1-1-s2-write-or-update-the-iac-module
    skills: [infrastructure-as-code, immutable-infrastructure, ephemeral-environments]
    reviewers: [infrastructure-reviewer, architecture-reviewer]
    output: "docs/iac-change.md"
    checkpoint: review-at-end
    on:
      "Quota or network blocked → delivery lead": authority
  - id: s3
    do: "Plan and review the change"
    owner: "Platform engineer"
    agent: "draft, then wait for review"
    command: build-4-1-1-1-s3-plan-and-review-the-change
    reviewers: [security-reviewer, vendor-reviewer]
    output: "docs/iac-change.md"
    checkpoint: review-at-end
  - id: d1
    decision: "Plan as expected — nothing unexpected destroyed?"
    owner: "Tech lead"
    agent: "prepare a decision brief — never decide"
    checkpoint: decision   # stop; Tech lead decides
    branches:
      "yes": s4
      "Unexpected change → fix the module": s2
      "Constraint unmeetable → back to DESIGN": stop
  - id: s4
    do: "Apply through the pipeline"
    owner: "CI/CD pipeline"
    agent: "draft, then wait for review"
    command: build-4-1-1-1-s4-apply-through-the-pipeline
    skills: [gitops]
    reviewers: [devops-reviewer]
    output: "docs/iac-change.md"
    checkpoint: review-at-end
    on:
      "Apply fails → re-plan": s3
  - id: s5
    do: "Record in the catalogue; schedule drift detection"
    owner: "Platform engineer"
    agent: "draft, then wait for review"
    command: build-4-1-1-1-s5-record-in-the-catalogue-schedule-drift-detection
    skills: [drift-detection]
    reviewers: [infrastructure-reviewer]
    output: "docs/environment-catalogue.md"
    checkpoint: review-at-end
gate: "Environment Ready"
criteria:
  - "Defined in code"
  - "Data class stated"
  - "Applied by the pipeline"
checks:
  - "Second-person plan review"
  - "Drift detection scheduled"
on_failure:
  - "Re-plan and re-apply from the last good commit"
  - "Reconcile drift in code, then re-apply"
rework: "Plan shows unexpected changes → correct the module and re-plan"
outputs:
  - "docs/environment-catalogue.md"
  - "docs/iac-change.md"
handoff: "Environment catalogue & IaC change records → 4.1.2 Build the CI/CD Pipeline"
learning:
  - "Parity gaps that later hid a defect — learning log"
```

files.title: Subprocess 4.1.1 · Provision Environments with Infrastructure as Code
files.body:
# Subprocess 4.1.1 · Provision Environments with Infrastructure as Code

Give the team environments it can trust: built from code, alike enough that what passes in staging behaves the same in production.

**Run it:** ask your agent to "run `workflows/build-4-1-1-environments.md` for {{initiative}}, stopping at every checkpoint", or use the command `build-4-1-1-run-environments`. Each checkpoint means: show me the output and wait. At `decision` checkpoints the named person decides.

```yaml
orchestration: build-4-1-1-environments
title: "Provision Environments with Infrastructure as Code"
owner: "Platform engineer"
inputs:
  - "docs/architecture-description.md"
  - "docs/qa-scenarios.md"
  - "docs/design-readiness-record.md"
entry:
  - "Architecture description and NFRs available"
  - "Hosting platform and accounts granted"
runs:
  - unit: "4.1.1.1 Provision an Environment from Code"
    spec: workflows/build-4-1-1-1-provision-env.md
    command: build-4-1-1-1-run-provision-env
    gate: "Environment Ready"
    checkpoint: review   # show outputs, wait for go-ahead
parallel:
  - "Environment modules ∥ pipeline stages (4.1.2)"
  - "Secrets paths prepared with 4.1.3"
gate: "Environment Ready"
decided_by: "Tech lead approves the environment set; platform engineer approves each apply; destroys in shared environments need the tech lead."
criteria:
  - "Every environment defined in code"
  - "Data class stated per environment"
  - "Parity gaps named"
routes:
  forward: "→ 4.1.2 Build the CI/CD Pipeline"
  rework: "Plan shows unexpected destroys → back to the IaC module"
  alternate: "Shared dev unusable → ephemeral environments per pull request"
  escalate: "Hosting or network access blocked → delivery lead"
  stop: "Platform cannot meet a hard constraint (e.g. data residency) → stop and return to DESIGN — recorded in the learning log"
outputs:
  - "docs/environment-catalogue.md"
  - "docs/iac-change.md"
handoff: "Environment catalogue & IaC change records → 4.1.2 Build the CI/CD Pipeline"
```

files.title: Workflow 4.1.2.1 · Define the Pipeline and Its Gates
files.body:
# Workflow 4.1.2.1 · Define the Pipeline and Its Gates

Stand up a protected repository and a pipeline-as-code whose gates enforce every automatable DoD item, proven by a walking skeleton.

**Run it:** ask your agent to "run `workflows/build-4-1-2-1-pipeline.md` for {{initiative}}, stopping at every checkpoint", or use the command `build-4-1-2-1-run-pipeline`. Each checkpoint means: show me the output and wait. At `decision` checkpoints the named person decides.

```yaml
workflow: build-4-1-2-1-pipeline
title: "Define the Pipeline and Its Gates"
owner: "Tech lead"
inputs:
  - "docs/environment-catalogue.md"
  - "docs/definition-of-done.md"
preconditions:
  - "Environments catalogued"
  - "DoD agreed"
steps:
  - id: s1
    do: "Create repository, standards and branch protection"
    owner: "Tech lead"
    agent: "draft, then wait for review"
    command: build-4-1-2-1-s1-create-repository-standards-and-branch-protection
    skills: [branch-protection, trunk-based-development]
    reviewers: [engineering-reviewer, security-reviewer]
    output: "docs/repo-standards.md"
    checkpoint: review-at-end
    on:
      "No usable CI platform → stop": stop
  - id: s2
    do: "Write the pipeline stages as code"
    owner: "Platform engineer"
    agent: "draft, then wait for review"
    command: build-4-1-2-1-s2-write-the-pipeline-stages-as-code
    skills: [pipeline-as-code, deployment-pipeline, continuous-integration-and-delivery]
    reviewers: [devops-reviewer, infrastructure-reviewer]
    output: "docs/pipeline-definition.md"
    checkpoint: review-at-end
    on:
      "Tool not approved → platform owner": authority
  - id: s3
    do: "Map each automatable DoD item to a failing gate"
    owner: "Tech lead"
    agent: "draft, then wait for review"
    command: build-4-1-2-1-s3-map-each-automatable-dod-item-to-a-failing-gate
    skills: [quality-gates]
    reviewers: [quality-reviewer, security-reviewer]
    output: "docs/pipeline-definition.md"
    checkpoint: review-at-end
  - id: s4
    do: "Run a walking-skeleton change end to end"
    owner: "Developer"
    agent: "draft, then wait for review"
    command: build-4-1-2-1-s4-run-a-walking-skeleton-change-end-to-end
    skills: [build-once-deploy-many]
    reviewers: [architecture-reviewer]
    output: "docs/pipeline-run.md"
    checkpoint: review-at-end
  - id: d1
    decision: "Every gate fails correctly and the run is under target?"
    owner: "Tech lead"
    agent: "prepare a decision brief — never decide"
    checkpoint: decision   # stop; Tech lead decides
    branches:
      "yes": gate
      "A gate passes when it should fail → re-map": s3
      "Too slow → parallelise or split stages": s2
gate: "Pipeline Ready"
criteria:
  - "Each automatable DoD item gated"
  - "PR checks < 10 min"
checks:
  - "Known-bad change rejected by each gate"
on_failure:
  - "Seed a known-bad change and prove each gate fails"
  - "Measure stages and parallelise the slowest"
rework: "A gate that lets a known-bad change through → re-map to the DoD"
outputs:
  - "docs/pipeline-definition.md"
  - "docs/repo-standards.md"
  - "docs/pipeline-run.md"
handoff: "Pipeline definition, repository standards & first green CI run → 4.1.3 Manage Secrets & Access"
learning:
  - "Gates that missed a defect — learning log"
```

files.title: Workflow 4.1.2.2 · Restore a Red Mainline
